```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 3.5, dpi = 96)
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

This page runs one analysis from start to finish, repeats it with a model
that adjusts for a covariate, and lists the arguments every function shares.
The other six functions return the same kind of object, with the same
`$notes`, `$emmeans`, `$posthoc` and `plot()`.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("elkronos/anovakit", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

```{r library}
library(anovakit)
```

## A first analysis

`mtcars` records the fuel economy (`mpg`) of 32 cars with 4, 6 or 8
cylinders. The question is whether mean fuel economy differs by cylinder
count.

```{r data}
table(mtcars$cyl)
round(tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, sd), 2)
```

The 4-cylinder cars vary far more than the 6-cylinder ones, so the comparison
should not assume equal variances. `anova_welch()` does not.

```{r welch}
fit <- anova_welch(mtcars, "mpg", "cyl")
fit
```

`cyl` is numeric in `mtcars`; grouping columns are converted to factors.

The printed result has four parts: the call and the number of rows used, the
omnibus test, the notes, and the names of the plots that were built.

### The notes

`$notes` records what the function decided on your behalf, what it could not
compute, and anything that changes how a number should be read.

```{r welch-notes}
fit$notes
```

Here it reports the variance ratio, which is the reason to use Welch's test.
On other data it would say how many rows were dropped for missing values, or
that a check could not run. Read it before you report anything from a fit.

### The summary

`summary()` adds the assumption checks, effect sizes, group summaries and
pairwise comparisons.

```{r welch-summary}
summary(fit)
```

The assumption checks are the ones that fit the method. Welch's test allows
unequal variances, so normality is tested within each group, not on pooled
residuals. The effect sizes are Hedges' g on the average of the two group
variances (the `standardiser` column gives the formula), with intervals. The
pairwise comparisons are Welch t tests; `p_value` is unadjusted and
`p_adjusted` uses Holm's method, the default for `anova_welch()`.

Every table is a data frame you can use directly:

```{r welch-tables}
fit$posthoc[, c("group1", "group2", "difference", "conf_low", "conf_high",
                "p_adjusted")]
```

### A plot

Plots are built when you fit and returned as `ggplot2` objects. Nothing is
drawn until you print one.

```{r welch-plot}
plot(fit, "means")
```

## The same analysis with a covariate

Heavier cars use more fuel, and the 8-cylinder cars are the heaviest. An
ANCOVA compares the cylinder groups at the same weight (`wt`, in thousands of
pounds).

```{r ancova}
anc <- anova_ancova(mtcars, "mpg", "cyl", "wt")
anc
```

```{r ancova-numbers, include = FALSE}
wt_means <- tapply(mtcars$wt, mtcars$cyl, mean)
wt_sd <- sqrt(sum(tapply(mtcars$wt, mtcars$cyl,
                         function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2))) / (nrow(mtcars) - 3))
wt_gap <- diff(range(wt_means)) / wt_sd
wt_max4 <- max(mtcars$wt[mtcars$cyl == 4])
wt_min8 <- min(mtcars$wt[mtcars$cyl == 8])
```

The call has the same shape, with the covariate as the fourth argument. The
notes record four things:

- `wt` was mean-centred at `r f3(anc$covariate_means[["wt"]])`. The model
  is additive, so centring changes only the intercept, and `$emmeans` are
  evaluated at that mean weight either way. Centring matters when the model
  includes the group-by-covariate term.
- The homogeneity-of-slopes test gave p = `r f3(anc$slopes_test$p_value)`, so
  the function fitted the additive model, and the p-values do not allow for
  that choice.
- The groups' mean weights differ by up to `r f2(wt_gap)` pooled
  within-group standard deviations, which makes the adjusted comparisons
  sensitive to a slope difference the test may have missed.
- The heaviest 4-cylinder car weighs `r f3(wt_max4)`, less than the average
  car, so the marginal mean for that group is an extrapolation.

These are observational data, and the notes say how far the adjusted
comparison leans on the model. The marginal means and comparisons are in the
same places as before:

```{r ancova-tables}
anc$emmeans
anc$posthoc[, c("contrast", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high",
                "p_adjusted")]
```

The covariate plot draws the fitted model (solid lines, one common slope)
and each group's own least-squares line (dashed) over the data. The
4-cylinder cars (at most `r f3(wt_max4)`) and the 8-cylinder cars (at least
`r f3(wt_min8)`) barely overlap in weight.

```{r ancova-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(anc, "covariate")
```

To fix the model in advance instead of letting the slopes test choose it,
set `force_interaction = TRUE`. The [ANCOVA walkthrough](articles/ancova.html)
covers that choice, the slopes test and covariate centring.

## Arguments every function shares

Each function takes the data first and names columns as character strings.
`anova_manova()` takes `responses` (plural), and `anova_rm()` takes
`response` with `subject`, `within` and `between`. These arguments mean the
same thing wherever they appear:

| Argument | Accepted by | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `conf_level` | all eight | `0.95` | The level of every interval in the returned tables. |
| `adjust` | all eight | `"holm"` (welch), `"BH"` (kw), `"tukey"` (the rest) | The multiplicity adjustment for the pairwise comparisons. |
| `posthoc` | all eight | `TRUE` | `FALSE` skips the pairwise comparisons, with a note (in `anova_welch()` this also empties `$effect_sizes`). The six model-based functions also skip them, with a note, above 5000 comparisons. |
| `plots` | all eight | `TRUE` | `FALSE` skips building the figures, which is faster. |
| `verbose` | all eight | `FALSE` | Progress messages through `message()`. |
| `interaction` | ancova, manova, bin, count, glm | `FALSE` (`TRUE` in ancova) | Additive, full factorial, or interactions up to a given order. |
| `type` | ancova, rm (through `...`), manova, bin, count, glm | `"II"` (`"III"` in ancova and rm) | Type II or Type III tests; `"III"` fits the model under sum-to-zero contrasts. |
| `covariates` | ancova, manova | none in manova (required in ancova) | Numeric columns to adjust for. |
| `vcov_type` | ancova, bin, count, glm | `"model"` | `"HC0"` to `"HC4"` gives sandwich standard errors. |
| `weights` | bin, count, glm | `NULL` | Prior weights, named as a column. |

`anova_welch()` and `anova_kw()` accept the `p.adjust()` methods for
`adjust`. The other six compare through emmeans and also accept `"tukey"`,
`"sidak"`, `"scheffe"` and `"dunnettx"`. Arguments specific to one function
are on its help page and in its walkthrough.
